title: Top Salary In The Company
description:
Report the single highest salary in the company.

Name the column `top_salary`. The result is exactly one row (NULL if there are no employees).
solutionSql: SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_salary FROM employees;
hint: A bare aggregate always returns exactly one row, even with no data — which is why MAX beats ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 here.
outputExplanation: The highest salary in the company is $150,000.
schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE departments (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  location TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  title TEXT,
  salary INTEGER,
  dept_id INTEGER,
  manager_id INTEGER,
  hire_date TEXT
);

tests.name: Department with no employees
Employees with NULL department and NULL salary
Single employee, single department
tests.seedSql:
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1,'Engineering','Austin');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Solo','Engineer',100000,1,NULL,'2022-04-01');

tests.name: Duplicate names and same hire dates
Zero and negative salaries, boundary dates
All NULL salaries — MAX returns NULL
tests.seedSql:
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1,'IT','A');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'A','X',NULL,1,NULL,'2020-01-01'),(2,'B','X',NULL,1,1,'2020-01-01');

tests.name: Single employee
tests.seedSql:
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1,'IT','A');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Solo','X',50000,1,NULL,'2020-01-01');

tests.name: Tie at the top — multiple employees share the max
Mix of negative and positive salaries
Mix of NULLs and values — NULLs are excluded
tests.seedSql:
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1,'IT','A');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'A','X',NULL,1,NULL,'2020-01-01'),(2,'B','X',300,1,1,'2020-01-01'),(3,'C','X',NULL,1,1,'2020-01-01');
